t: True or false? Participation in community life is one of the fundamental principles of British life.
e: Participation in community life is one of the five fundamental principles of British life, alongside democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and tolerance. The handbook encourages everyone to get involved, for example by volunteering or helping in local groups.

t: True or false? You can take the Life in the UK test at any college or school.
e: You cannot take the test at any college or school. It must be taken at a registered and approved Life in the UK test centre, booked online.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Everyone living in the UK is expected to respect and obey the law.
Only British citizens are expected to obey the law.
e: Everyone living in the UK, not just citizens, is expected to respect and obey the law. This is one of the responsibilities of living in the UK.

t: Besides passing the Life in the UK test, what else is usually needed to apply for settlement or citizenship?
o: Evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level or above
A British sponsor for every year of residence
e: To apply for settlement or citizenship you usually need to pass the Life in the UK test and show you can speak and listen in English at B1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference, or above. A degree, sponsor or driving licence is not required.

t: True or false? People on work visas normally must pass the Life in the UK test to become permanent residents.
e: The Life in the UK test is usually taken by people who want to become permanent residents or citizens, including those who came on work visas. They must also show their English language ability.

t: What do you need to apply for settlement in the UK? (Choose TWO)
o: A pass in the Life in the UK test
Evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level
e: To apply for settlement you usually need to pass the Life in the UK test and show evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level or above. A driving licence or British spouse is not required.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Tolerance of those with different faiths is a fundamental principle of British life.
Following the state religion is a fundamental principle of British life.
e: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle of British life. There is no requirement to follow any state religion.

t: Where can you book the Life in the UK test?
o: By phone to the Home Office
e: You can only book the Life in the UK test online, at an approved test centre. There are about 60 test centres around the UK.

t: Which of these is part of the citizenship pledge?
o: "I will live in the UK for the rest of my life"
e: The citizenship pledge includes 'I will observe its laws faithfully'. The full pledge also promises loyalty to the UK, respect for its rights and freedoms, upholding its democratic values, and fulfilling your duties and obligations as a British citizen.

t: The Life in the UK test questions need an understanding of English at which level?
e: The questions are written so that they need an understanding of English at ESOL Entry Level 3. Separately, applicants for settlement or citizenship usually need evidence of English speaking and listening at B1 level.

t: Which of these is part of the pledge new citizens make?
o: "I will join the armed forces if asked"
"I will attend a place of worship"
"I will always vote for the government"
e: The citizenship pledge is: 'I will give my loyalty to the United Kingdom and respect its rights and freedoms. I will uphold its democratic values. I will observe its laws faithfully and fulfil my duties and obligations as a British citizen.'

t: Before October 2013, what was the alternative to taking the Life in the UK test for people with lower English?
o: An ESOL course in English with Citizenship
e: The Life in the UK test was one way of showing knowledge of life in the UK. Until October 2013, people with lower levels of English could instead take an ESOL (English for Speakers of Other Languages) course in English with Citizenship.

t: Which TWO countries have devolved parliaments or assemblies?
e: Scotland has a Parliament and Wales an Assembly, each with devolved powers; Northern Ireland also has an Assembly. England does not have its own devolved parliament, and the Isle of Man is not part of the UK.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Falkland Islands are a British overseas territory.
The Falkland Islands are a Crown dependency.
e: The Falkland Islands are a British overseas territory, like St Helena. Crown dependencies are the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man.

t: True or false? British overseas territories such as St Helena are part of the UK.
e: British overseas territories, such as St Helena and the Falkland Islands, have strong links with the UK but are not part of it.

t: Which part of the island of Ireland is an independent country?
o: The rest of Ireland outside Northern Ireland
e: The island of Ireland is divided. Northern Ireland, in the north-east, is part of the UK. The rest of the island is the Republic of Ireland, an independent country.

t: What are the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man called?
e: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are called Crown dependencies. They have their own governments and have a special relationship with the UK. The Falkland Islands and St Helena are British overseas territories.

t: True or false? The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man have their own governments.
e: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies with their own governments. They have a special relationship with the UK but are not part of it, and they make many of their own laws.

t: Which countries make up Great Britain?
o: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
e: Great Britain is the name for the island containing England, Scotland and Wales. The United Kingdom is Great Britain plus Northern Ireland. A common mistake is to think Great Britain includes Northern Ireland; it does not.

t: Which TWO of these are Crown dependencies, not part of the UK?
e: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies. They have a close relationship with the UK and the monarch, but they have their own governments and are not part of the UK. The Isle of Wight and Anglesey are islands that are part of the UK.

t: Which of these is a British overseas territory?
e: The handbook names the Falkland Islands and St Helena as British overseas territories. The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies, and Iceland is an independent country.

t: Which TWO of these are British overseas territories named in the handbook?
e: The handbook names St Helena and the Falkland Islands as British overseas territories, which have strong links with the UK but are not part of it. The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown dependencies, a different category.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Boudicca was queen of the Iceni.
e: Boudicca was the queen of the Iceni, a tribe in what is now eastern England, and fought against the Romans. There is a statue of her on Westminster Bridge.

t: In which year was the National Health Service established?
e: The National Health Service (NHS) began in 1948 under the post-war Labour government. It guaranteed a minimum standard of healthcare for all, free at the point of use.

t: Missionaries led by St Augustine came from where?
e: St Augustine led missionaries from Rome who spread Christianity in the south of England. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

t: Roughly how long did the Romans stay in Britain?
e: The Romans arrived successfully in AD 43 and left in AD 410 to defend other parts of their empire, so they stayed for about 400 years. During this time they built roads and public buildings, created a legal structure and introduced new plants and animals.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Hadrian's Wall was built to keep out the Picts.
Hadrian's Wall was built to keep out the Vikings.
e: The Roman Emperor Hadrian had a wall built in the north of England to keep out the Picts, the ancestors of the Scottish people. The Vikings came much later.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: In 1918, women over 30 were given the right to vote.
In 1918, women over 18 were given the right to vote.
e: In 1918, women over the age of 30 were given the right to vote. In 1928 the voting age for women was lowered to 21, the same as men.

t: Which TWO social measures were introduced before the First World War?
e: Before the First World War, Britain introduced a number of social reforms, including free school meals, old-age pensions and support for people who were unemployed. The NHS and free secondary education came after the Second World War.

t: In the Middle Ages, people came to England with special skills. Where did the glass manufacturers come from?
e: In the Middle Ages, people came to England from abroad with special skills: weavers from France, engineers from Germany, glass manufacturers from Italy and canal builders from Holland.

t: Until when did the British Empire continue to grow?
e: The British Empire continued to grow until the 1920s. After the Second World War, many countries gained independence and the Empire gradually became the Commonwealth.

t: In 1847, the working hours of women and children were limited to how many hours a day?
e: Working conditions improved in the 19th century. In 1847 the number of hours that women and children could work was limited by law to 10 hours per day.

t: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and which wife?
e: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn. She was a Protestant who re-established the Church of England, and she became one of the most popular monarchs in English history.

t: Sir Bernard Lovell built a radio telescope at which place?
e: Research into radar led to the development of radio astronomy. Sir Bernard Lovell built a radio telescope at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire, which was for many years the biggest in the world.

t: Which architect designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire?
e: After the Great Fire of London in 1666, Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral and many other churches. St Paul's is still a famous feature of the London skyline.

t: What was the Easter Rising of 1916?
o: An uprising in Dublin against the British
e: In 1916 there was an uprising, the Easter Rising, against the British in Dublin. Its leaders were executed under military law, and a guerrilla war followed, leading to the partition of Ireland in 1922.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.
Inigo Jones designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.
e: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of 1666. Inigo Jones designed the Queen's House at Greenwich.

t: When did the BBC begin the world's first regular television service?
e: The BBC started radio broadcasts in 1922 and began the world's first regular television service in 1936.

t: In 1990, Britain helped liberate which country after it was invaded by Iraq?
e: In 1990, Britain was involved in the international coalition that liberated Kuwait after it was invaded by Iraq. Later, in 2003, British forces took part in the invasion of Iraq.

t: Who became Prime Minister after Labour won the 1945 election?
e: The Labour Party won the 1945 general election, and Clement Attlee became Prime Minister. His government created the NHS and nationalised major industries.

t: Which TWO facts are true about Clement Attlee?
o: He was Churchill's Deputy Prime Minister in the wartime coalition
He led the Labour Party for 20 years
He was Prime Minister from 1960 to 1970
e: Clement Attlee was Churchill's Deputy Prime Minister in the wartime coalition government and led the Labour Party for 20 years. He was Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.

t: True or false? Elizabeth I asked people about their real religious beliefs and punished those who disagreed.
e: Elizabeth I did not ask about people's real beliefs. She succeeded in finding a balance between the views of Catholics and more extreme Protestants, which helped avoid serious religious conflict in England during her reign.

t: In which year was there a revolution in France?
e: There was a revolution in France in 1789, and the new French government soon declared war on Britain. The wars with Napoleon ended with his defeat at Waterloo in 1815.

t: How long did Queen Victoria reign?
e: Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837 aged 18 and reigned until 1901, almost 64 years. Her reign was the longest of any monarch at that time, and is known as the Victorian period.

t: Before becoming an MP, Churchill was which TWO things?
e: Before becoming an MP, Winston Churchill was a soldier and a journalist. He became a Conservative MP in 1900.

t: Rudyard Kipling won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907. Which book did he write?
e: Rudyard Kipling, born in India in 1865, wrote books and poems set in India and the UK, including The Jungle Book and the poem 'If'. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

t: Roughly how many casualties did the British suffer on the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916?
e: The handbook says the British suffered 60,000 casualties on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916, making it one of the bloodiest battles of the First World War.

t: In which year was there a major outbreak of plague in London?
e: In 1665 there was a major outbreak of plague in London, and thousands of people died, especially in poorer areas. A year later, in 1666, the Great Fire of London destroyed much of the city.

t: Which TWO kings believed in the "Divine Right of Kings"?
e: James I and his son Charles I believed in the 'Divine Right of Kings', the idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule. This led to conflict with Parliament and, eventually, the English Civil War.

t: Sake Dean Mahomet opened the first curry house in Britain in 1810. What was it called?
e: Sake Dean Mahomet came to Britain from India and in 1810 opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in George Street, London, the first curry house in Britain. He also introduced 'shampooing' (Indian head massage) to Britain.

t: What was built to link factories to towns, cities and ports during the Industrial Revolution?
e: Better transport links were needed to carry raw materials and manufactured goods. Canals were built to link factories to towns and cities and to the ports, particularly in the middle and north of England.

t: What language did the Norman ruling class speak?
e: After the Norman Conquest, the king and his noblemen spoke Norman French, while peasants continued to speak Anglo-Saxon. Over time the two languages combined to become English.

t: By about which year were Anglo-Saxon kingdoms established in Britain?
e: The languages of the Jutes, Angles and Saxons are the basis of modern-day English. By about AD 600, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were established in Britain, mainly in what is now England.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Adam Smith developed ideas about economics.
Adam Smith invented the steam engine.
e: Adam Smith was a thinker of the Scottish Enlightenment who developed ideas about economics that are still referred to today. James Watt worked on steam power.

t: What does the cross of St Patrick look like?
o: A red diagonal cross on a white ground
A red cross on a white ground
A white diagonal cross on a blue ground
A green cross on a white ground
e: The cross of St Patrick, patron saint of Ireland, is a red diagonal cross on a white ground. It was added to the Union Flag in 1801.

t: Which TWO writers were prominent in the inter-war period?
e: The inter-war period saw many developments in the arts and literature. Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh were prominent writers of this time. Dickens and Austen wrote in the 19th century.

t: When did Winston Churchill become Prime Minister?
e: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940, after Germany invaded Belgium, the Netherlands and France. He led Britain through the war and refused to surrender.

t: Under the Bill of Rights, how often did a new Parliament have to be elected?
e: The Bill of Rights stated that a new Parliament had to be elected at least every three years. This later became every seven years, and it is now at least every five years.

t: Between 1853 and 1913, how many British citizens left the country?
e: Between 1853 and 1913, as many as 13 million British citizens left the country. At the same time, people also came to Britain, including Jewish people fleeing persecution in Russia.

t: In what year did King John agree to Magna Carta?
e: In 1215, King John was forced by his noblemen to agree to Magna Carta (the Great Charter). It established the idea that even the king was subject to the law and protected the rights of the nobility, restricting the king's power to collect taxes or change laws.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
e: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564.

t: Which TWO industries developed during the 1930s?
e: Despite the Great Depression, new industries developed in the 1930s, such as the automobile and aviation industries. Older heavy industries, like shipbuilding and coal, suffered badly.

t: In 2002, who was voted the greatest Briton of all time?
e: Winston Churchill was voted the greatest Briton of all time by the public in 2002. He led Britain during the Second World War and was famous for his speeches.

t: What was the Blitz?
o: The German bombing of British cities at night
e: After losing the Battle of Britain, Germany bombed London and other British cities at night. This was called the Blitz. Coventry was almost totally destroyed, but the population kept strong and refused to surrender.

t: True or false? The Domesday Book still exists today.
e: The Domesday Book still exists today. It was made for William I and recorded the towns and villages in England, who lived there, who owned the land and what animals they owned.

t: Which Prime Minister after Margaret Thatcher helped establish the Northern Ireland peace process?
e: John Major was Prime Minister after Margaret Thatcher, from 1990 to 1997. He helped to establish the Northern Ireland peace process, which later led to the Good Friday Agreement under Tony Blair in 1998.

t: Who was Prime Minister for most of the Second World War?
e: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940 and led Britain through the Second World War. He refused to surrender to the Nazis and was known for inspiring speeches. He was Prime Minister again from 1951 to 1955.

t: Who invented the theoretical "Turing machine"?
e: In the 1930s the British mathematician Alan Turing invented the theoretical 'Turing machine', which led to the development of the modern computer. He also worked on breaking codes in the Second World War.

t: True or false? The Beatles and The Rolling Stones were popular groups in the 1960s.
e: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones were popular British bands in the 1960s, a period known as 'the Swinging Sixties'.

t: After the Glorious Revolution, who could vote for Members of Parliament?
o: Only men who owned property of a certain value
e: After the Glorious Revolution, only men who owned property of a certain value could vote. Women could not vote at all, and some constituencies (rotten or pocket boroughs) were controlled by a few people.

t: For how many years was Britain a republic?
e: England was a republic from 1649, when Charles I was executed, to 1660, when Charles II was restored: 11 years. It was called the Commonwealth, and Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector.

t: Where was Anne Boleyn executed?
e: Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife and the mother of Elizabeth I, was English. She was unpopular in the country and was executed at the Tower of London.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Act of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.
The Act of Union of 1707 united Great Britain and Ireland.
e: The Act of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain by uniting England and Scotland. Ireland was united with Great Britain in 1801.

t: In which year did Guy Fawkes and the Gunpowder Plot try to blow up Parliament?
e: In 1605 a group of Catholics led by Guy Fawkes plotted to blow up the Houses of Parliament and kill the Protestant king, James I. The plot failed, and people still mark it every 5 November with fireworks on Bonfire Night.

t: Where was the author Roald Dahl born?
e: Roald Dahl was born in Wales to Norwegian parents. He served in the Royal Air Force during the Second World War and later wrote children's books such as Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and George's Marvellous Medicine.

t: Which TWO things did Protestants do differently from Roman Catholics?
o: Read the Bible in their own languages
Did not pray to saints or at shrines
Accepted the authority of the Pope
e: Protestants formed their own churches. They read the Bible in their own languages instead of Latin, did not pray to saints or at shrines, and believed a person's own relationship with God was more important than submitting to the Church's authority.

t: When was the Northern Ireland Assembly suspended, before being reinstated in 2007?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly was set up after the Good Friday Agreement of 1998. It was suspended in 2002 and reinstated in 2007.

t: Which Dylan Thomas poem was written for his dying father?
o: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night
e: Dylan Thomas wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night' for his dying father. His radio play Under Milk Wood is also very well known.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Bill of Rights confirmed the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power.
The Bill of Rights allowed the king to raise taxes without Parliament.
e: The Bill of Rights of 1689 confirmed the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power. The king could not raise taxes without Parliament's agreement.

t: What is Robert Burns known as in Scotland?
e: Robert Burns (1759–96) is known in Scotland as 'The Bard'. He was a Scottish poet, and his best-known work is 'Auld Lang Syne'.

t: True or false? The jet engine was invented by John Logie Baird.
e: The jet engine was developed by Sir Frank Whittle. John Logie Baird developed television.

t: True or false? The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1688.
e: The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588, not 1688. 1688 was the year of the Glorious Revolution.

t: When did English settlers first begin to colonise the eastern coast of America?
o: In the time of Elizabeth I
In the time of Henry VIII
e: In Elizabeth I's time, English settlers first began to colonise the eastern coast of America. This colonisation, as well as immigration to North America, increased greatly in the 17th century.

t: Which scientist, an early member of the Royal Society, predicted the return of a comet?
e: Sir Edmund Halley, an early member of the Royal Society, successfully predicted the return of the comet now called Halley's Comet. Sir Isaac Newton was another famous early member.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Mary, Queen of Scots was a Catholic.
Mary, Queen of Scots was a Protestant.
e: Mary, Queen of Scots was a Catholic. She was forced to give up her throne to her Protestant son, James VI.

t: In which year did Argentina invade the Falkland Islands?
e: In 1982 Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic. A naval task force was sent from the UK, and military action led to the recovery of the islands.

t: Which king, a Roman Catholic, came to the throne in 1685?
e: Charles II had no legitimate children and died in 1685. His Catholic brother James became King James II in England, Wales and Ireland, and James VII in Scotland.

t: In the medieval English Parliament, who was elected to the House of Commons?
o: Knights and wealthy people from towns and cities
e: In the medieval English Parliament, knights (usually smaller landowners) and wealthy people from towns and cities were elected to the House of Commons. The nobility, great landowners and bishops sat in the House of Lords.

t: Which of these statements about the suffragettes is NOT true?
o: They won the vote for all women in 1900
They campaigned for women's right to vote
Emmeline Pankhurst helped found the WSPU
e: The suffragettes did not win the vote for all women in 1900. Women over 30 got the vote in 1918, and women got the vote at the same age as men (21) in 1928.

t: To whom did Mary, Queen of Scots give her throne?
e: Mary, Queen of Scots was forced to give up her throne to her Protestant son, James VI. She then fled to England, where she was held prisoner by Elizabeth I for 20 years.

t: True or false? The Normans invaded and conquered Scotland in 1066.
e: The Normans invaded England in 1066 but did not conquer Scotland. Scotland remained independent.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998.
The Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1972.
e: The Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998. 1972 was when the Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended.

t: At the coronation of William and Mary, what was read out?
e: At the coronation of William and Mary, a Declaration of Rights was read out. It confirmed that the king would not raise taxes or administer justice without agreement from Parliament, and became law as the Bill of Rights in 1689.

t: "All the world's a stage" comes from which Shakespeare play?
e: 'All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players' is from As You Like It. Other famous Shakespeare lines include 'Once more unto the breach' from Henry V.

t: In 1932, John Logie Baird made the first television broadcast between which two cities?
e: In 1932, John Logie Baird made the first television broadcast between London and Glasgow. He had developed television in the 1920s.

t: What did Iron Age people make that marks the beginnings of British history?
o: The first coins minted in Britain
e: Iron Age people made the first coins to be minted in Britain, some inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings. This marks the beginnings of British history, because it is the first written evidence of who ruled.

t: Who was reigning when Wales became formally united with England?
e: Wales became formally united with England by the Act for the Government of Wales during the reign of Henry VIII.

t: After the Civil War, who was given the title Lord Protector?
e: After the Civil War England had no king and was a republic. Oliver Cromwell, the army leader, was given the title of Lord Protector and ruled until his death in 1658.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: More than 300,000 men were rescued from the beaches around Dunkirk.
About 3,000 men were rescued from the beaches around Dunkirk.
e: More than 300,000 men were rescued from the beaches around Dunkirk in 1940, many using civilian volunteer boats.

t: Who was one of the commanders in the defeat of the Spanish Armada?
e: Sir Francis Drake was one of the commanders in the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588. He was one of the founders of England's naval tradition.

t: Until 1870, what happened to a woman's earnings and property when she married?
o: They automatically belonged to her husband
e: Until 1870, when a woman got married, her earnings, property and money automatically belonged to her husband. Acts of Parliament in 1870 and 1882 gave wives the right to keep their own earnings and property.

t: In 1969 the voting age was lowered to what?
e: In 1969 the voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 for men and women. It is still 18 for UK Parliament elections.

t: What does the phrase "the Dunkirk spirit" come from?
o: The evacuation of soldiers from France in 1940
e: In 1940, more than 300,000 men were rescued from the beaches around Dunkirk, in France, using civilian volunteer boats. The phrase 'the Dunkirk spirit' is still used to describe people pulling together in a crisis.

t: With which country did Britain often come into conflict over trade and colonies in the 18th century?
e: In the 18th century Britain often came into conflict with France, which also wanted to trade and colonise in the same areas. This led to wars, including those with Napoleon.

t: In 2010, which two parties formed a coalition government?
e: In May 2010, for the first time since 1974, no party won an overall majority. The Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats formed a coalition government, and David Cameron became Prime Minister.

t: Under feudalism, what were most peasants?
o: Serfs who worked for their lord and could not move away
e: Under feudalism, most people were peasants. Many were serfs: they had a small area of their lord's land where they could grow food, and in return worked for their lord and could not move away.

t: True or false? Henry VIII married six times.
e: Henry VIII married six times: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard and Catherine Parr.

t: True or false? In the Middle Ages the principle that judges are independent of the government began to be established.
e: In the Middle Ages, the legal system also changed. The idea that judges are independent of the government began to be established, which is still an important principle today.

t: What were the "plantations" in Ireland?
o: Settlements of Scottish and English Protestants on land taken from Catholics
e: During Elizabeth I's reign and afterwards, English and Scottish Protestants were encouraged to settle in Ireland on land confiscated from Catholic landholders. These settlements were known as plantations, and many settlers went to the province of Ulster.

t: About how long ago did Britain become permanently separated from the continent by the Channel?
e: The first people to live in Britain were hunter-gatherers, in the Stone Age. For much of that time Britain was connected to the continent by a land bridge. Britain became permanently separated from the continent by the Channel about 10,000 years ago.

t: Where did most slaves transported on British ships come from?
e: Most slaves transported on British ships were from West Africa. They were taken to America and the Caribbean, where they worked in terrible conditions on tobacco and sugar plantations.

t: When did the Irish Free State become a republic?
e: The Irish Free State became a republic in 1949. Northern Ireland remained part of the UK.

t: Where can the Bayeux Tapestry be seen today?
e: The Bayeux Tapestry, which commemorates the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings, can still be seen today in France.

t: Which TWO methods did the suffragettes use?
o: Forming a political party in government
e: The suffragettes used civil disobedience as part of their protest. They chained themselves to railings, smashed windows and committed arson. Many went on hunger strike when sent to prison.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Domesday Book listed towns, villages and landowners in England.
The Domesday Book was a collection of Anglo-Saxon poems.
e: The Domesday Book, made for William I, listed the towns and villages in England, who lived there, who owned the land and what animals they owned. It still exists today.

t: Which TWO countries were among the Axis powers?
e: The Axis powers in the Second World War were fascist Germany and Italy, and the Empire of Japan. Poland was invaded by Germany, and Canada fought with the Allies.

t: Why is Oliver Cromwell still a controversial figure in Ireland?
o: He established Parliament's authority there with great violence
He made Ireland a separate kingdom
e: Cromwell went to Ireland to establish the authority of the English Parliament. He did this with great violence, including the massacres at Drogheda and Wexford, so he is still a controversial figure in Ireland.

t: True or false? Charles II hid in an oak tree after the Battle of Worcester.
e: After being defeated by Cromwell at the Battle of Worcester in 1651, Charles II famously hid in an oak tree on one occasion, before escaping to Europe.

t: What was Isaac Newton's most famous published work?
e: Isaac Newton's most famous published work was Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica ('Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy'). It showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

t: Who co-discovered insulin, used to treat diabetes?
e: The Scottish scientist John MacLeod was the co-discoverer of insulin, which is used to treat diabetes.

t: What does "universal suffrage" mean?
o: The right of every adult, male or female, to vote
The right of property owners to vote
The right to join a trade union
e: 'Universal suffrage' means the right of every adult, male or female, to vote. It was achieved gradually, with women gaining equal voting rights in 1928.

t: Roughly how many people lived in the British Empire at its height?
e: During the Victorian period the British Empire grew to cover all of India, Australia and large parts of Africa. It became the largest empire the world has ever seen, with an estimated population of more than 400 million people.

t: Who did the Scots declare to be king after Charles I was executed?
e: After Charles I was executed, the Scots did not agree and declared his son, Charles II, to be king. He was crowned in Scotland, but Cromwell's army defeated him.

t: What does the official Welsh flag show?
e: The official Welsh flag shows a Welsh dragon. It does not appear on the Union Flag because Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created in 1606.

t: Which of Henry VIII's wives was a cousin of Anne Boleyn and was also executed?
e: Catherine Howard, a cousin of Anne Boleyn, was Henry VIII's fifth wife. She was accused of taking lovers and was also executed.

t: In what year was a peace treaty signed leading to the split of Ireland?
e: A guerrilla war followed the Easter Rising, and in 1921 a peace treaty was signed. In 1922 Ireland became two countries: the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland, which stayed part of the UK.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Habeas Corpus Act guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully.
The Habeas Corpus Act gave women the right to vote.
e: The Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully. Women did not get the vote until 1918.

t: Which TWO books were written by Roald Dahl?
e: Roald Dahl wrote many children's books, including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and George's Marvellous Medicine. The Jungle Book is by Kipling and Treasure Island by Robert Louis Stevenson.

t: What was Stonehenge probably used for?
o: A special gathering place for seasonal ceremonies
A burial place for Viking kings
e: Stonehenge, in Wiltshire, was probably a special gathering place for seasonal ceremonies. It was built by the first farmers, about 6,000 years ago onwards, and still stands today.

t: What was the Reformation?
o: A movement against the authority of the Pope and the Roman Catholic Church
A reform of the voting system
The rebuilding of London after the Great Fire
e: The Reformation was a movement against the authority of the Pope and the ideas and practices of the Roman Catholic Church. The Protestants formed their own churches, read the Bible in their own languages and prayed directly to God.

t: Which religious group set up the first formal anti-slavery groups?
e: The Quakers set up the first formal anti-slavery groups. Later, William Wilberforce, an MP, helped change the law. Trading in slaves was abolished in 1807, and slavery itself in the British Empire in 1833.

t: From 1695, what could newspapers do for the first time?
e: Since 1695, newspapers have been allowed to operate without a government licence. Increasing numbers of newspapers began to be published after that.

t: Why was Hadrian's Wall built?
o: To mark the border with Wales
e: The Roman Emperor Hadrian had a wall built in the north of England to keep out the Picts, the ancestors of the Scottish people. Parts of Hadrian's Wall, including forts such as Housesteads and Vindolanda, can still be seen today.

t: The Wars of the Roses were fought between which two houses?
e: In 1455 a civil war began to decide who should be king of England. It was fought between the House of Lancaster, whose symbol was a red rose, and the House of York, whose symbol was a white rose, so it became known as the Wars of the Roses.

t: Who is the spiritual leader of the Church of England?
e: The Archbishop of Canterbury is the spiritual leader of the Church of England. The monarch is the head (Supreme Governor) of the Church and has the right to select the Archbishop and other senior officials.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Diwali is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs.
e: Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs. The Jewish festival of lights is Hannukah.

t: Which TWO are modern British architects?
e: Modern British architects include Sir Norman Foster, Lord (Richard) Rogers and Dame Zaha Hadid, who have worked on major projects around the world. Inigo Jones and Robert Adam were 17th- and 18th-century architects.

t: Where is the Scottish Grand National held?
e: The Scottish Grand National is held at Ayr. The Grand National itself is held at Aintree, near Liverpool.

t: True or false? More women than men study at university in the UK.
e: On average, girls leave school with better qualifications than boys, and more women than men study at university. Women work in all sectors of the economy.

t: Which of these is a UK coin rather than a banknote?
e: The coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2. The notes are £5, £10, £20 and £50.

t: What discount on a TV licence can blind people get?
e: People over 75 can apply for a free TV licence, and blind people can get a 50% discount. The money from licences pays for the BBC.

t: Which composer wrote the Pomp and Circumstance Marches?
e: Sir Edward Elgar, born in Worcester, England, wrote the Pomp and Circumstance Marches. March No 1 (Land of Hope and Glory) is usually played at the Last Night of the Proms.

t: Which TWO foods are traditionally eaten on Christmas Day?
e: On Christmas Day people usually eat a special meal, which often includes roast turkey, Christmas pudding and mince pies. Pancakes are eaten on Shrove Tuesday, and haggis is traditional in Scotland.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Mousetrap was written by Agatha Christie.
The Mousetrap was written by Andrew Lloyd Webber.
e: The Mousetrap, a murder-mystery play, was written by Agatha Christie and has run in the West End since 1952. Andrew Lloyd Webber writes musicals.

t: How many pence are there in a pound?
e: The currency in the UK is the pound sterling (symbol £). There are 100 pence in a pound.

t: Who was the first person to sail around the world single-handed without stopping?
e: Sir Robin Knox-Johnston became the first person to sail around the world single-handed and non-stop, in 1968/69. Sir Francis Chichester had done it single-handed but with a stop, two years earlier.

t: Roughly what share of the UK population lives in Scotland?
e: England makes up about 84% of the UK's population, Scotland just over 8%, Wales around 5% and Northern Ireland less than 3%.

t: What language do some people in Northern Ireland speak?
e: In Northern Ireland, some people speak Irish Gaelic. There are also different accents and dialects across the UK.

t: Sir Chris Hoy is a champion in which sport?
e: Sir Chris Hoy is a Scottish cyclist who has won six Olympic gold medals and 11 world championship titles.

t: What is the biggest and best-known part of the Edinburgh Festival?
e: The Edinburgh Festival takes place in Edinburgh every summer. It includes many different arts festivals, and the biggest and best known is the Edinburgh Festival Fringe ('the Fringe').

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world.
Wimbledon is played on clay courts.
e: Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and the only 'Grand Slam' event played on grass, not clay.

t: Where did the Paralympic Games originate?
e: The Paralympic Games have their origins in the work of Dr Sir Ludwig Guttmann at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in Buckinghamshire, who developed new methods of treatment for people with spinal injuries and encouraged them to take part in sport.

t: What do people sometimes send on Valentine's Day to someone they secretly admire?
e: Valentine's Day, 14 February, is when lovers exchange cards and gifts. Sometimes people send anonymous cards to someone they secretly admire.

t: Which TWO items are part of an Ulster fry?
e: Ulster fry, from Northern Ireland, is a fried meal with bacon, eggs, sausage, black pudding, white pudding, tomatoes, mushrooms, soda bread and potato bread.

t: Where is the city of Newport?
e: Newport is a city in Wales, along with Cardiff (the capital) and Swansea.

t: Which event is marked by a public holiday in Northern Ireland in July?
o: The anniversary of the Battle of the Boyne
e: In Northern Ireland, the anniversary of the Battle of the Boyne, where William III defeated James II in 1690, is a public holiday in July.

t: Which TWO events did Mo Farah win gold in at the 2012 Olympics?
e: At the 2012 Olympic Games in London, Mo Farah won gold medals in the 5,000 metres and the 10,000 metres. He was the first Briton to win the Olympic gold in the 10,000 metres.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
e: Henry Moore (1898–1986) was an English sculptor, best known for his large bronze abstract sculptures.

t: Which of these statements about Big Ben is NOT true?
o: The clock tower was renamed the Victoria Tower in 2012
Big Ben is the nickname for the great bell of the clock
The clock is over 150 years old
The clock tower is named the Elizabeth Tower
e: The clock tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower, not the Victoria Tower, in 2012, in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee. Big Ben is the nickname for the great bell.

t: Roughly what share of the UK population lives in Wales?
e: Wales makes up around 5% of the UK's population. England has about 84%, Scotland just over 8% and Northern Ireland less than 3%.

t: Which flower is associated with England?
e: The rose is associated with England. The other national flowers are the thistle (Scotland), the daffodil (Wales) and the shamrock (Northern Ireland).

t: What are the two types of rugby?
e: There are two types of rugby, rugby union and rugby league. Both have separate leagues and national teams in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (which plays with the Irish Republic).

t: Where was the first tennis club founded, in 1872?
e: Modern tennis evolved in England in the late 19th century. The first tennis club was founded in Leamington Spa in 1872. The most famous tournament today is Wimbledon.

t: In which county is Stoke Mandeville hospital?
e: Stoke Mandeville hospital, where the Paralympics began through the work of Dr Sir Ludwig Guttmann, is in Buckinghamshire.

t: Which TWO cities are in Scotland?
e: Dundee and Aberdeen are cities in Scotland, along with Edinburgh, Glasgow and Inverness. Newport is in Wales and Norwich is in England.

t: True or false? On April Fool's Day, people play jokes on each other until midday.
e: On April Fool's Day, 1 April, people play jokes on each other until midday. The television and newspapers often have stories that are April Fool jokes.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day.
Boxing Day is the day before Christmas Day.
e: Boxing Day, 26 December, is the day after Christmas Day and is a public holiday. Christmas Eve is the day before Christmas.

t: What does Good Friday mark?
o: The rising of Jesus Christ from the dead
e: Good Friday marks the death of Jesus Christ. Easter Sunday celebrates his rising from the dead. Both Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays.

t: What was the UK population in 1901?
e: The UK population grew fast in the 19th century. It was 8 million in 1801, 20 million in 1851 and 40 million in 1901.

t: Who decides the hours a pub or night club is open?
e: The licensee (the person licensed to sell alcohol) decides the hours a pub or night club is open, within the terms of their licence.

t: In Scotland, which extra day after New Year is a public holiday?
e: Hogmanay (New Year's Eve) is a big celebration in Scotland, and 2 January is also a public holiday there. In the rest of the UK, 1 January is the only New Year public holiday.

t: Nearly what share of the UK population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK?
e: Nearly 10% of the population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK. The UK population is ethnically diverse and changing rapidly, especially in large cities.

t: Who usually chooses the Archbishop of Canterbury?
o: The Prime Minister and a committee appointed by the Church
A vote of all church members
e: The monarch has the right to select the Archbishop and other senior church officials, but usually the choice is made by the Prime Minister and a committee appointed by the Church.

t: In the 2009 Citizenship Survey, what percentage of people identified as Christian?
e: In the 2009 Citizenship Survey, 70% of people identified themselves as Christian. Much smaller proportions identified as Muslim (4%), Hindu (2%), Sikh, Jewish or Buddhist (less than 1% each).

t: Which country hosted the 1966 World Cup?
e: England hosted the football World Cup in 1966 and won it, captained by Bobby Moore. It is the only time England has won the World Cup.

t: What is Boxing Day?
e: Boxing Day is 26 December, the day after Christmas Day, and is a public holiday. Christmas Day celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ.

t: When is Halloween?
e: Halloween, 31 October, is an ancient festival with roots in the pagan festival to mark the beginning of winter. Young people dress up in frightening costumes and play 'trick or treat', and people carve lanterns out of pumpkins.

t: What is the capital city of Wales?
e: Cardiff is the capital city of Wales. The capitals of the other UK countries are London (England), Edinburgh (Scotland) and Belfast (Northern Ireland).

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Football is the UK's most popular sport.
Cricket is the UK's most popular sport.
e: Football is the UK's most popular sport. Cricket is also popular, but is not the most popular.

t: John Petts, a Welsh artist, is best known for what?
e: John Petts (1914–91) was a Welsh artist, best known for his engravings and stained glass.

t: Which TWO are famous UK music festivals?
e: Festival season takes place across the UK every summer. Famous music festivals include Glastonbury, the Isle of Wight Festival and the V Festival.

t: What is the name for the 40 days before Easter?
e: The 40 days before Easter are known as Lent. It is a time when Christians take time to reflect and prepare for Easter, and traditionally fast; today many people give up something they enjoy.

t: Jane Austen's novels are concerned with what?
e: Jane Austen (1775–1817) was an English novelist. Her books, such as Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility, are concerned with marriage and family relationships.

t: Which composer wrote The Planets?
e: Gustav Holst wrote The Planets, a suite of pieces themed around the planets and their astrological signs. His work often included folk tunes.

t: Which TWO poets wrote about their experiences in the First World War?
e: Many poets were inspired to write about their experiences in the First World War. Some of the most famous are Wilfred Owen, who wrote 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', and Siegfried Sassoon.

t: What is the maximum fine for watching TV without a TV licence?
e: Everyone in the UK with a TV, computer or other device used to watch or record programmes as they are broadcast must have a TV licence. You can be fined up to £1,000 if you watch TV without one.

t: Which TWO novels were written by Evelyn Waugh?
e: Evelyn Waugh (1903–66) wrote satirical novels, including Decline and Fall and Scoop. He is perhaps best known for Brideshead Revisited.

t: What is the Turner Prize awarded for?
e: The Turner Prize, named after the painter Joseph Mallord William Turner, was established in 1984 and celebrates contemporary art. It is one of the most prestigious visual art awards in Europe.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Proms is an eight-week summer season of classical music.
The Proms is an annual horse race.
e: The Proms is an eight-week summer season of orchestral classical music, organised by the BBC since 1927. It takes place at venues including the Royal Albert Hall.

t: What do Easter eggs symbolise?
e: At Easter, people give eggs, usually made of chocolate, as a symbol of new life. Easter celebrates the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

t: "She walks in beauty, like the night" was written by which poet?
e: 'She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies' is from the poem 'She Walks in Beauty' by Lord Byron.

t: Which TWO are popular British soap operas?
e: Coronation Street and EastEnders are popular British soap operas, which follow the lives of families and communities. Spitting Image and Monty Python are comedy shows.

t: Where was the main site of the 2012 Olympic Games?
e: The main Olympic site for the 2012 Games was in Stratford, East London. The UK was also the first country to host the modern Paralympic Games, in 2012 in London.

t: When is St Andrew's Day?
e: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland, and St Andrew's Day is 30 November. The other patron saints' days are St David (Wales) 1 March, St Patrick (Northern Ireland) 17 March and St George (England) 23 April.

t: What is roast beef traditionally served with in England?
e: A traditional English meal is roast beef, served with potatoes, vegetables, Yorkshire puddings (batter that is baked in the oven) and other accompaniments.

t: Lucian Freud is best known for which kind of work?
e: Lucian Freud (1922–2011) was a German-born British artist. He is best known for his portraits.

t: Which artist is considered to have raised the profile of landscape painting?
e: Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775–1851) was an influential landscape painter in a modern style. He is considered the artist who raised the profile of landscape painting. The Turner Prize is named after him.

t: True or false? Shops and businesses must accept Scottish and Northern Irish banknotes.
e: Northern Ireland and Scotland have their own banknotes, which are valid everywhere in the UK. However, shops and businesses do not have to accept them.

t: Who give tours at the Tower of London?
e: The Tower of London was first built by William the Conqueror after he became king in 1066. Tours are given by the Yeoman Warders, also known as Beefeaters, who tell visitors about its history. The Crown Jewels are kept there.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
e: Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival, celebrated on 14 April, that marks the founding of the Sikh community known as the Khalsa.

t: Which architect designed the Cenotaph in Whitehall?
e: Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the Cenotaph in Whitehall, which is the site of the annual Remembrance Day service. He had a great influence on buildings in New Delhi, India.

t: Which TWO drivers are recent British Formula 1 world champions?
e: There have been several British Formula 1 world champions, including Damon Hill, Lewis Hamilton and Jensen Button. Andy Murray is a tennis player and Mo Farah a runner.

t: Which architect designed the Queen's House at Greenwich?
e: In the 17th century, Inigo Jones took inspiration from classical architecture to design the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House in Whitehall, London.

t: How tall is the London Eye?
e: The London Eye is 135 metres tall. It is situated on the southern bank of the River Thames and was originally built as part of the UK's celebration of the new millennium. It continues to be a major attraction.

t: Who often worked with Edwin Lutyens to design colourful gardens?
e: Gertrude Jekyll often worked with Sir Edwin Lutyens to design colourful gardens around the houses he designed.

t: What was the UK population in 1951?
e: The UK population was 50 million in 1951, 57 million in 1998, just under 60 million in 2005 and just over 62 million in 2010.

t: True or false? St George's Day is an official public holiday in England.
e: St George's Day, 23 April, is not an official public holiday in England. Only St Andrew's Day (Scotland) and St Patrick's Day (Northern Ireland) are public holidays.

t: What is the day before Lent starts called?
e: The day before Lent starts is Shrove Tuesday, also called Pancake Day. People eat pancakes, which were traditionally made to use up food such as eggs before fasting. The first day of Lent is Ash Wednesday.

t: Where is the Millennium Stadium?
e: The Millennium Stadium in Cardiff is the home of the Welsh rugby team. The UK has many famous sports venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.

t: Who captained the England team that won the World Cup in 1966?
e: England won the football World Cup in 1966, captained by Bobby Moore. It was the only time England has won the World Cup.

t: "Tyger! Tyger! Burning bright" was written by which poet?
e: 'Tyger! Tyger! burning bright / In the forests of the night' is from 'The Tyger' by William Blake.

t: Hardwick Hall, a great country house, is in which county?
e: In the 16th century, great country houses were built, such as Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire. English country house architecture then developed further in the 17th and 18th centuries.

t: Which TWO famous gardens are in England?
e: Famous gardens in England include Kew Gardens, Sissinghurst and Hidcote. Bodnant Garden is in Wales, and Mount Stewart is in Northern Ireland.

t: In 2010, the UK population was...
e: In 2010 the UK population was just over 62 million. Population growth has been faster in recent years, partly because of migration and longer life expectancy.

t: Which of these statements about pubs is NOT true?
o: Anyone aged 14 or over can buy alcohol in a pub
You must be 18 to buy alcohol in a pub
People aged 16 can drink wine or beer with a meal if with someone over 18
e: You must be 18 or over to buy alcohol in a pub. People aged 16 can drink wine or beer with a meal in a hotel or restaurant if they are with someone over 18.

t: Where is Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park?
e: Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park, in the west of Scotland, covers 720 square miles. Loch Lomond is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain.

t: What is the minimum age to buy alcohol in the UK?
e: You must be 18 or over to buy alcohol. People aged 16 or over can drink wine or beer with a meal in a hotel or restaurant if they are with someone over 18.

t: Roughly what share of the UK workforce is made up of women?
e: Women in Britain today make up about half of the workforce. On average, girls leave school with better qualifications than boys, and more women than men study at university.

t: Who founded the Aldeburgh festival in Suffolk?
e: Benjamin Britten is best known for his operas, including Peter Grimes and Billy Budd. He also founded the Aldeburgh festival in Suffolk, which continues to be a popular music event of international importance.

t: Where can you get vaccinations and medical treatment for animals?
e: Vaccinations and medical treatment for animals are available from veterinary surgeons (vets). There are charities that may help people who cannot afford to pay a vet.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Loch Lomond is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain.
Loch Ness is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain.
e: Loch Lomond is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain. It is in the west of Scotland.

t: When were films first shown publicly in the UK?
e: Films were first shown publicly in the UK in 1896, and film screenings very quickly became popular. From the beginning, British film makers became famous for clever special effects.

t: Whose books introduced James Bond?
e: Ian Fleming's books introduced James Bond. The James Bond films are one of the two highest-grossing film franchises, alongside Harry Potter.

t: Which city is the capital of Scotland?
e: Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland, and is where the Scottish Parliament sits, at Holyrood. Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, but it is not the capital.

t: Which organisation collects income tax and National Insurance?
o: The Department for Work and Pensions
e: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) is the government department that collects taxes. Income tax and National Insurance are usually taken from wages automatically by employers through the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) system.

t: Who are "the judiciary"?
e: Judges are known as 'the judiciary'. They are responsible for interpreting the law and ensuring that trials are conducted fairly. They are independent of the government.

t: Who decides the verdict in a Magistrates' Court?
e: In a Magistrates' Court, the magistrates decide the verdict (whether the defendant is guilty) and, if guilty, the sentence. There is no jury.

t: What is the minimum age to vote in a UK general election?
e: The present voting age of 18 was set in 1969. Both men and women aged 18 or over can vote in UK Parliament elections, provided they are registered.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy.
The Home Secretary is responsible for the economy.
e: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy. The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.

t: What is a special constable?
e: A special constable is a volunteer police officer who works with the regular police. It is one of several ways people can volunteer to support their community and the justice system.

t: True or false? It is a criminal offence to cause harassment, alarm or distress to someone because of their religion or ethnic origin.
e: It is a criminal offence to cause harassment, alarm or distress to someone because of their religion or ethnic origin. Everyone in the UK has the right to be protected from this.

t: True or false? Taking a girl abroad for FGM is a criminal offence.
e: Female genital mutilation (FGM) is illegal in the UK. Practising FGM, or taking a girl or woman abroad for FGM, is a criminal offence.

t: Which TWO countries were founding members of the European Economic Community?
e: The EEC was founded in 1957 by six countries: West Germany, France, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. The UK joined later, in 1973, and Ireland joined at the same time.

t: Criminal law relates to crimes usually investigated by whom?
o: The police or another authority such as a council
e: Criminal law relates to crimes, which are usually investigated by the police or another authority such as a council, and which are punished by the courts.

t: Which TWO of these are civil law matters?
o: A dispute between a landlord and tenant over repairs
e: Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups, such as housing disputes between landlords and tenants and employment issues like unfair dismissal. Selling alcohol to under-18s and carrying a knife are criminal offences.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The UK has a constitutional monarchy.
The UK has an absolute monarchy.
e: The UK has a constitutional monarchy. The monarch is head of state, but government policy is decided by elected politicians.

t: When should you put your rubbish bags and bins on the street?
o: Only when they are due to be collected
e: You should make sure your rubbish bags and bins are put on the street only when they are due to be collected. Being considerate of your neighbours is part of community life.

t: Which of these statements about the police is NOT true?
o: Police officers may be rude if they think a suspect is guilty
The police protect life and property
The police are independent of the government
e: Police officers must not be rude or abusive, whatever they think of a suspect. The police must obey the law and not misuse their authority.

t: How many local authorities does London have?
e: Towns, cities and rural areas are governed by elected councils. London has 33 local authorities, with the Greater London Authority and the Mayor of London coordinating policies across the capital.

t: What are solicitors?
o: Trained lawyers who give legal advice and represent clients
e: Solicitors are trained lawyers who give advice on legal matters, take action for their clients and represent them in court. Their charges are usually based on how much time they spend on a case.

t: True or false? Members of the House of Lords are elected by the public.
e: Members of the House of Lords are not elected by the public. They are appointed (life peers), elected among themselves (some hereditary peers) or sit as senior bishops.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: It is a criminal offence to carry a weapon of any kind, even for self-defence.
You may carry a knife in public if it is for self-defence.
e: It is a criminal offence to carry a weapon of any kind, even if it is for self-defence.

t: What is the Council of Europe responsible for?
o: Protecting and promoting human rights in its member countries
e: The Council of Europe is separate from the EU. It has 47 member countries, including the UK, and is responsible for protecting and promoting human rights in those countries. It has no power to make laws but draws up conventions and charters, such as the European Convention on Human Rights.

t: True or false? Members of the House of Lords may stand for election to the House of Commons.
e: Members of the House of Lords (peers) may not stand for election to the House of Commons. Members of the armed forces and civil servants are also not allowed to stand.

t: Which TWO things do Police and Crime Commissioners do?
e: Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) are elected by the public in areas of England and Wales. They set local police priorities and the local policing budget, and appoint the local Chief Constable.

t: How many countries are members of the United Nations?
e: The UK is part of the United Nations (UN), an international organisation with more than 190 countries as members. It was set up after the Second World War to prevent war and promote international peace and security.

t: True or false? You can vote by post if you register for a postal ballot.
e: If it is difficult for you to get to a polling station, you can register for a postal ballot and vote by post.

t: Which TWO were demands of the Chartists?
o: For any man to be able to stand as an MP
e: The Chartists' demands included elections every year, for any man to be able to stand as an MP, for every man to have the vote, secret ballots, equal-sized electoral districts and paid MPs. They did not call for votes for women or an end to the monarchy.

t: True or false? Local councils provide services such as education, housing and waste collection.
e: Towns, cities and rural areas are governed by local councils. They provide services such as education, housing, waste collection, libraries, social services and roads. Funding comes from central government and local taxes.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
The Human Rights Act was agreed by King John in 1215.
e: The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. Magna Carta was agreed by King John in 1215.

t: Since which year have some powers been devolved to Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland?
e: Since 1997, some powers have been devolved from the central government to give people in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland more control over matters that directly affect them.

t: Which document, drawn up by the Council of Europe, sets out rights that member states protect?
o: The European Convention on Human Rights
e: The UK was one of the first countries to sign the European Convention on Human Rights, drawn up by the Council of Europe. It sets out rights such as the right to life, freedom of thought and the right to a fair trial.

t: Where in the UK must you show photographic ID at a polling station?
e: The handbook says that in Northern Ireland you must show photographic identification at a polling station before you can vote.

t: When are most local council elections held?
e: Most local council elections are held in May every year. Many candidates stand for council election as members of a political party.

t: If an accused person is aged between 10 and 17, which court normally hears the case?
e: If an accused person is aged 10 to 17, the case is normally heard in a youth court in front of up to three specially trained magistrates or a district judge. The public cannot attend, and the young person's name cannot be published.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: You must have your name on the electoral register to vote.
You can vote without being on the electoral register.
e: To vote in a UK election, you must have your name on the electoral register. You can register through your local council.

t: What should you do if you think someone is trying to persuade you to join an extremist or terrorist cause?
e: If you think someone is trying to persuade you to join an extremist or terrorist cause, you should notify your local police force. Extremism has no place in British society.

t: According to the handbook, how many member states does the EU have?
e: The handbook says the EU has 28 member states. The test follows the handbook, so 28 is the answer to give.

t: Since which year has the UK had a fully democratic voting system?
e: The UK has had a fully democratic voting system since 1928, when women were given the vote at 21, the same age as men. The voting age was later reduced to 18 in 1969.

t: Which charity works with older people?
e: Age UK is a charity that works with older people. The handbook gives examples of charities that work with children (NSPCC), the homeless (Crisis, Shelter), animals (PDSA) and the environment (National Trust, Friends of the Earth).

t: Where does the Scottish Parliament sit?
e: The Scottish Parliament sits in Edinburgh, the capital of Scotland, in a building at Holyrood. It was formed in 1999 and can pass laws for Scotland on matters not reserved to the UK Parliament.

t: When were Police and Crime Commissioners first elected?
e: In November 2012 the public elected Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) in England and Wales for the first time. They are responsible for the delivery of an efficient and effective police force in their area.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: The police are independent of the government.
The police take orders directly from the Prime Minister.
e: The police are independent of the government. Each force is headed by a Chief Constable.

t: True or false? You must tell a canvasser how you intend to vote.
e: Voting in the UK is secret. When canvassers visit, you can discuss issues with them, but you do not have to tell them how you intend to vote.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Defence and foreign affairs remain under the control of the UK government.
The Scottish Parliament controls defence for Scotland.
e: Defence and foreign affairs, along with immigration, taxation and social security, remain under the control of the UK government. They are not devolved.

t: In Northern Ireland, who hears cases in the Magistrates' Courts?
o: A District Judge or Deputy District Judge
e: In Northern Ireland, cases in the Magistrates' Courts are heard by a District Judge or Deputy District Judge, who is legally qualified and paid. In England and Wales, magistrates are usually unpaid volunteers.

t: What happens every week while Parliament is sitting, giving the opposition a chance to challenge the government?
e: Every week while Parliament is sitting, the Prime Minister answers questions from MPs, including the Leader of the Opposition, in Prime Minister's Questions. It is an important opportunity for the opposition to challenge the government.

t: True or false? By law, radio and television coverage of political parties must be balanced.
e: The UK has a free press, and newspaper owners can express political opinions. However, by law, radio and television coverage of political parties must be balanced, so each party is given similar amounts of time.

t: What does the CBI represent?
e: Pressure and lobby groups try to influence government policy. The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) represents the views of British business.

t: True or false? The House of Commons has powers to overrule the House of Lords.
e: The House of Commons has powers to overrule the House of Lords, but these are not used often. The Commons is the more important chamber because its members are elected.

t: How does voter registration work in Northern Ireland?
o: Each person completes their own form (individual registration)
e: The handbook says that in Northern Ireland a system called 'individual registration' is used, where each person fills in their own registration form. Elsewhere, one form was sent to each household.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: You must be at least 17 years old to drive a car.
You must be at least 21 years old to drive a car.
e: You must be at least 17 years old to drive a car or motorcycle, and 16 to ride a moped.

t: Which TWO can the Northern Ireland Assembly make decisions on?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly can make decisions on issues such as education, agriculture, the environment, health and social services. Defence and immigration stay with the UK government.

t: What is the title of the heir apparent to the throne?
e: The heir to the throne has the title Prince of Wales. The monarch is head of state of the UK, and the role passes to the heir apparent.

t: What is the opposition?
o: The second-largest party in the House of Commons
e: The second-largest party in the House of Commons is called the opposition. The Leader of the Opposition usually becomes Prime Minister if their party wins the next General Election.

t: Which TWO kinds of income is income tax paid on?
e: Income tax is paid on wages from paid employment, profits from self-employment, taxable benefits, pensions, and income from property, savings and dividends.

t: What does "extremism" mean in the handbook?
o: Vocal or active opposition to fundamental British values
Being a member of a political party
e: The handbook describes extremism as vocal or active opposition to fundamental British values, such as democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs.

t: Which TWO policy areas remain under central UK government control?
e: Some policy and legislative areas remain under the central UK government, including defence, foreign affairs, immigration, taxation and social security. Education and health have been devolved to Scotland and Wales.

t: Until 1958, which TWO groups were members of the House of Lords?
o: Bishops of the Church of England
e: Until 1958, all peers in the House of Lords were hereditary peers (people who inherited their title) or senior judges or bishops of the Church of England. Life peers were introduced in 1958.

t: What does the handbook suggest when you move into a new home?
o: Put your bins out every day
Ask the council for a welcome visit
e: When you move into a new house or apartment, it is a good idea to introduce yourself to the people who live near you. Getting to know your neighbours helps you become part of the community.

t: Which TWO must follow the principles of the European Convention on Human Rights?
e: The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. Government, public bodies and the courts must follow its principles.

t: Which TWO are ways parents can help at their children's school?
e: Parents can help their children's school in many ways, such as helping in the classroom, listening to children read, and joining the parent-teacher association (PTA), which organises events and raises money.

t: How many members does the Scottish Parliament have?
e: The Scottish Parliament has 129 members (MSPs), elected by a form of proportional representation. It sits in Edinburgh, the capital of Scotland.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Criminal law relates to crimes; civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups.
Civil law relates to crimes; criminal law is used to settle disputes between individuals.
e: Criminal law relates to crimes, which are investigated by the police and punished by the courts. Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups.

t: Which TWO are benefits of volunteering mentioned in the handbook?
o: A chance to practise your English
Developing work skills for your CV
e: Volunteering helps others and gives you a chance to practise your English, develop work skills for your CV and meet new people. It is unpaid work.

t: What are the Commonwealth's core values?
o: Democracy, good government and the rule of law
Free trade, a common currency and shared defence
e: The Commonwealth is based on the core values of democracy, good government and the rule of law. It has no power over its members, and membership is voluntary.

t: Where must a car be registered if you are resident in the UK?
o: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)
e: If you are a UK resident, your car or motorcycle must be registered at the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA). You must pay an annual vehicle tax and display the tax disc; you must also have insurance.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Youth Courts hear cases of people aged 10 to 17.
Youth Courts hear cases of people aged 18 to 21.
e: Youth Courts hear cases of young people aged 10 to 17. Members of the public are not allowed in, and the young person's name cannot be published.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Magistrates in England and Wales usually work unpaid.
Magistrates in England and Wales must be qualified lawyers.
e: Magistrates in England and Wales usually work unpaid and do not need legal qualifications. They receive training to do the role.

t: Which TWO statements about the Speaker are true?
o: The Speaker is an MP and deals with constituents' problems
The Speaker represents Parliament on ceremonial occasions
The Speaker leads the governing party
The Speaker is appointed by the monarch
e: The Speaker is an MP who represents a constituency and deals with constituents' problems like any other MP. The Speaker also represents Parliament on ceremonial occasions, and is chosen by other MPs, not the monarch.

t: What are MPs' local "surgeries"?
o: Meetings where constituents can talk to them in person
e: Many MPs hold regular local 'surgeries', where constituents can go in person to talk about issues of concern. These are often advertised in the local newspaper.

t: What is the minimum age to be a school governor?
e: People who are 18 or over can become school governors (or school board members in Scotland). Governors are volunteers from the local community who help set the strategic direction of a school and hold the headteacher to account.

t: By which year had most of the Chartists' reforms been adopted?
e: The Chartists' campaign was generally seen as a failure at the time, but by 1918 most of their reforms had been adopted.

t: How often must a general election be held?
e: A general election must be held at least every five years. At a general election, MPs are elected to represent each of the 650 constituencies in the UK.

t: What happens if an MP dies or resigns?
o: A by-election is held in their constituency
The seat stays empty until the next General Election
e: If an MP dies or resigns, there will be a fresh election, called a by-election, in their constituency. This means the constituency is never left without an MP until the next General Election.

t: According to the handbook, how many member countries does the Council of Europe have?
e: The handbook says the Council of Europe has 47 member countries, including the UK. It is separate from the EU and works to protect and promote human rights.

t: True or false? It is a criminal offence to buy alcohol for someone under 18.
e: It is a crime to sell alcohol to anyone who is under 18 or to buy alcohol for people who are under the age of 18.

t: Since which year has the Welsh Assembly been able to pass laws without the UK Parliament's agreement?
e: Since 2011, the Welsh Assembly has been able to pass laws on its devolved areas without the agreement of the UK Parliament.

t: Which of these statements is correct?
o: Polling stations are open from 7.00 am until 10.00 pm.
Polling stations are open from 9.00 am until 5.00 pm.
e: Polling stations are open from 7.00 am until 10.00 pm on election day.

t: Where does the Scottish Parliament meet?
e: The Scottish Parliament meets in a building at Holyrood, in Edinburgh. It was formed in 1999 and can pass laws for Scotland on all matters not reserved to the UK Parliament.
